text.arabic_uthmani: مَا يُبَدَّلُ ٱلْقَوْلُ لَدَىَّ وَمَآ أَنَا۠ بِظَلَّٰمٍۢ لِّلْعَبِيدِ

words.gloss_range: opening negative particle over a passive verbal clause; selected as declarative negation, not relative or interrogative use
words.prose: {{ar:مَا}} ({{tr:mā}}) opens the ayah by negating the passive alteration clause, so the first movement is a categorical denial of revising the decree rather than a command, question, or past report. Its identical partner later at word 6 makes the ayah a two-denial structure: first what cannot happen to the word, then what cannot be predicated of the speaker. The long opening sound gives the negation audible weight before any noun appears.

topics.headline: opening negation scopes over passive alteration
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the ayah begins by excluding alteration as a standing fact, not by issuing another command or asking a question.
topics.reason: The following imperfect passive verb selects negative-particle force, and the clause is analyzed as a negated passive verbal clause.

topics.headline: two mā tokens build paired denials
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears and sees the ayah built from two matched negations, with verbal non-alteration paired to nominal non-oppression.
topics.reason: The first clause is verbal and the second clause is nominal, both opened by the same negative particle.

topics.headline: long opening negator carries recitational weight
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears negation as the ayah's launch, before the decree noun or the divine self-description arrives.
topics.reason: The row is phonetic rather than syntactic, but it has a local payoff because the first sound initiates the whole paired-denial frame.

words.gloss_range: Form II imperfect passive under negation: the decree is not altered, substituted, or tampered with, while no changer is named
words.root_gloss_range: replacement and alteration field, including exchange and substitution branches; local Form II passive selects denied external alteration of the decree, not mutual exchange or self-sought replacement

supporting_anchors.gloss_range: the definite word or decree as passive subject

words.prose: {{ar:يُبَدَّلُ}} ({{tr:yubaddalu}}) makes alteration impossible without naming any would-be changer: the passive promotes {{ar:ٱلْقَوْلُ}} ({{tr:al-qawlu}}) as the affected subject and closes the agency slot. The {{ar:ب د ل}} ({{tr:b-d-l}}) field gives the denied action the sharper sense of substitution or replacement, while the local Form II passive keeps the focus on external tampering with the decree rather than mutual exchange, self-transformation, or someone seeking a substitute. The verb also seals the prior warning as an irrevocable decree and stands inside the broader divine-word immutability field (6:34, 6:115, 18:27).

topics.headline: passive verb blocks changer-focused dispute
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the decree is protected regardless of who might try to change it, because the grammar suppresses the changer and negates the event itself.
topics.reason: The verb is Form II imperfect passive, with an unresolved suppressed agent and {{ar:ٱلْقَوْلُ}} ({{tr:al-qawlu}}) as passive subject.

topics.headline: replacement field sharpens the denied action
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees that the blocked change is not vague instability but replacement or substitution pressure against the decree.
topics.reason: The broader root family includes exchange, self-change, mutual exchange, and seeking replacement, but local Form II passive selects denied external alteration of the word.

topics.headline: verb joins divine-word immutability language
topics.reader_payoff: The reader connects this compact passive clause to the Quranic theme that divine words admit no changer (6:34, 6:115, 18:27), while noting the local wording uses a passive no-change predicate.
topics.reason: The distribution and parallels support a divine-speech immutability field without overriding the local passive syntax.

topics.headline: prior warning becomes irrevocable decree
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the warning mentioned just before 50:29 is no longer merely admonition; it is treated as the word that cannot be substituted.
topics.reason: Boundary rows tie the verb to the prior warning content and show the discourse turning speech into a protected decree-object.

topics.headline: compressed sound mirrors stopped substitution pressure
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears pressure inside the doubled middle of the verb before the stable decree noun arrives.
topics.reason: The phonetic rows add a local recitational payoff and remain subordinate to the grammar and root-field topics.

words.gloss_range: the definite word, speech, or decree; locally the prior divine warning treated as a binding decree and passive subject
words.root_gloss_range: speech, saying, utterance, and decree field; local syntax and context select an articulated divine decree rather than narrative report or generic talk
words.prose: {{ar:ٱلْقَوْلُ}} ({{tr:al-qawlu}}) is nominative as the passive subject, so the word itself stands in the subject slot while remaining the thing whose alteration is denied. Its definiteness points back to the prior warning and also lets the statement become a principle about binding divine speech. The noun keeps speech concrete: not a vague rule, but an articulated decree in the Surah Qaf speech chain (50:18, 50:23, 50:27, 50:28), aligned with wider no-change divine-word language (6:34, 6:115, 18:27).

topics.headline: definite decree is promoted as passive subject
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the decree is grammatically centered as the protected subject of the passive verb, not left as an implied object.
topics.reason: Case and attachment evidence identify the noun as the passive subject of {{ar:يُبَدَّلُ}} ({{tr:yubaddalu}}).

topics.headline: qawl is speech narrowed to binding decree
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears the word as articulated speech that has legal force, not as mere narrative report or an unspecified saying.
topics.reason: The root range covers saying and speech, but the passive alteration frame and 50:28 boundary select the juridical decree sense.

topics.headline: surah speech-chain and immutability parallels converge
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees this word as the decisive divine speech inside a local courtroom chain (50:18, 50:23, 50:27, 50:28) and a broader divine-word immutability pattern (6:34, 6:115, 18:27).
topics.reason: The inter-ayah rows give concrete local and cross-surah parallels, while the local noun remains {{ar:ٱلْقَوْلُ}} ({{tr:al-qawlu}}), not another speech noun.

topics.headline: decree noun anchors the middle of the first clause
topics.reader_payoff: The reader feels the decree noun as the hinge between denied alteration and the divine-presence phrase that follows.
topics.reason: The first clause defines the noun through a blocked event, then closes on the locative domain.

words.gloss_range: first-person locative adverb: before Me, with Me, in My presence; locally the divine jurisdiction where alteration fails

supporting_anchors.gloss_range: independent first-person pronoun in the second denial

words.prose: {{ar:لَدَىَّ}} ({{tr:ladayya}}) makes the non-alteration claim locative and jurisdictional: the word is not changed before the divine speaker, in the very domain where dispute was just forbidden (50:28). The fused first-person suffix keeps the same speaker anchored across the boundary, then the later independent {{ar:أَنَا۠}} ({{tr:ana}}) turns that domain claim into explicit self-description. The first clause therefore closes not only on a decree but on the speaker's immediate presence.

topics.headline: locative presence becomes jurisdiction
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that immutability is framed as what holds before the divine speaker, not as an abstract property detached from presence and authority.
topics.reason: The word is an adverbial locative attached to the passive verb, and the context is the courtroom-like divine address from 50:28.

topics.headline: fused first-person form repeats the prior divine anchor
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees 50:28 and 50:29 sharing the same divine-presence marker, so the prohibition of dispute and the decree's immutability belong to one scene.
topics.reason: The first-person suffix is discourse-inferred as the divine speaker and repeats the same locative anchor from 50:28.

topics.headline: final yā lets presence close the first beat
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears the first clause land on the divine locative, giving presence the final sound before the coordinated second denial begins.
topics.reason: The phonetic payoff is local and supports the clause-boundary topic.

words.gloss_range: coordinating conjunction linking the two complete negated clauses; additive, not oath or adversative contrast

supporting_anchors.gloss_range: first-person locative closing the first clause

words.prose: {{ar:وَ}} ({{tr:wa}}) joins two full negated clauses rather than launching an oath or a subordinate aside. The conjunction keeps the unchangeable-word claim and the non-oppression claim coordinate, while the sequence lets the second clause ground the first: finality and justice are paired, not opposed. Its short attached onset restarts the cadence after {{ar:لَدَىَّ}} ({{tr:ladayya}}) without severing the two halves.

topics.headline: wāw coordinates two complete negations
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the justice clause has equal declarative weight with the decree clause, instead of being an oath or incidental circumstance.
topics.reason: Clause evidence identifies coordination between two main negated clauses.

topics.headline: pivot pairs finality with justice
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the ayah's logic turn on this hinge: the decree is final, and the speaker who makes it is not oppressive.
topics.reason: The conjunction links a passive verbal denial to a nominal self-description, making the two claims mutually interpretive.

topics.headline: single-letter form restarts the second denial compactly
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears a light restart into the second {{ar:مَا}} ({{tr:mā}}), marking transition without a hard break.
topics.reason: The form and cadence rows have a local payoff at the clause boundary.

words.gloss_range: second negative particle in a nominal predicate construction; with the following bāʾ it strengthens denial of the oppressor predicate
words.prose: The second {{ar:مَا}} ({{tr:mā}}) looks like the first, but its grammar changes: it opens a nominal predicate denial with {{ar:أَنَا۠}} ({{tr:ana}}) and {{ar:بِظَلَّٰمٍ}} ({{tr:bi-ẓallāmin}}). That shift matters because the ayah now denies an attribute of the speaker, not an event involving the word. With the reinforcing bāʾ, the particle excludes the oppressor-description from the divine self while echoing the first negation to keep both halves categorical. The nasal chain through the negator, pronoun, and predicate also makes the second denial move as one recited unit before the servant phrase completes it.

topics.headline: second mā works with reinforced predicate
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the second negation is not bare denial; it belongs to a marked {{ar:مَا}} ({{tr:mā}}) plus bāʾ predicate construction.
topics.reason: The following bāʾ-marked predicate routes the parse toward the emphatic nominal-negation construction.

topics.headline: nominal denial targets characterization
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the ayah move from what cannot happen to the decree to what cannot be true of the speaker.
topics.reason: The word is followed by an explicit pronoun and predicate, not a verb, so the denial is an attribute claim.

topics.headline: repeated mā frames the whole ayah
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears the two halves as matched categorical denials even though their clause types differ.
topics.reason: The same surface particle opens both the verbal and nominal denial frames.

topics.headline: nasal sounds bind the nominal denial
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears the negator, pronoun, and predicate move as one recitational unit before the servant phrase completes it.
topics.reason: The sound row is local and supports the second-clause cohesion.

words.gloss_range: independent first-person pronoun serving as the explicit subject of the negated nominal clause

supporting_anchors.gloss_range: first-person locative in the preceding clause

words.prose: {{ar:أَنَا۠}} ({{tr:ana}}) gives the divine self-reference its own word slot between negation and predicate. The subject could have been inferred from context, but here it is explicit, so the denial of oppression is personally routed to the speaker rather than left as a general principle. Its open vowels let the self-reference be heard distinctly before the heavy predicate arrives. After the locative {{ar:لَدَىَّ}} ({{tr:ladayya}}), the discourse moves from where the decree stands to who cannot be described as oppressive.

topics.headline: explicit pronoun fixes the denied predicate to the speaker
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the justice guarantee is anchored in the divine speaker directly, not in an implied or generic subject.
topics.reason: The independent pronoun is the subject of the nominal negation and has the divine speaker as its discourse referent.

topics.headline: scene contracts into divine self-declaration
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the discourse leave the disputants of 50:28 and become an unopposed first-person declaration about divine character.
topics.reason: Boundary and discourse rows show the move from second-person disputation to first-person self-description.

topics.headline: detached form and open vowels foreground the self-reference
topics.reader_payoff: The reader hears and sees the pronoun as a distinct pause-worthy center before the heavy predicate arrives.
topics.reason: The independent form gives the self-reference a visible slot and a local cadence payoff.

words.gloss_range: reinforcing bāʾ on the negated predicate; governs genitive form while preserving predicative force

supporting_anchors.gloss_range: negative particle governing the nominal predicate construction
intensive predicate governed by reinforcing bāʾ
lām phrase naming the affected servant class

words.prose: {{ar:بِ}} ({{tr:bi}}) is not an instrumental by or with here. It enters the predicate in the {{ar:مَا}} ({{tr:mā}}) construction, gives {{ar:ظَلَّٰمٍ}} ({{tr:ẓallāmin}}) its visible genitive form, and strengthens the negation while the adjective remains a predicate. As a clitic it binds the negator and the intensive adjective before {{ar:لِلْعَبِيدِ}} ({{tr:li-l-ʿabīd}}) names the affected class, and the light particle hardens immediately into the emphatic predicate entry.

topics.headline: bāʾ reinforces the negated predicate
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the denial of oppression is grammatically marked and intensified, not expressed by a plain predicate alone.
topics.reason: The bāʾ is analyzed as reinforcing the predicate of the {{ar:مَا}} ({{tr:mā}}) clause while governing genitive case.

topics.headline: clitic binds negation to the intensive adjective
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees case, polarity, and predicate entry working together: the particle visibly attaches to the denied adjective and locks it into the construction.
topics.reason: The token is separate in analysis but fused in the written and recited predicate phrase.

words.gloss_range: intensive oppressor or habitual wrongdoer predicate under reinforced negation; locally denies any oppressor-character toward the servants
words.root_gloss_range: wronging, injustice, misplacement, and darkness-related imagery; local faʿʿāl predicate selects habitual or intensive oppression, while derivative darkness and accusation branches remain image-level background

supporting_anchors.gloss_range: lām phrase completing the denied oppression predicate

words.prose: {{ar:ظَلَّٰمٍ}} ({{tr:ẓallāmin}}) is the denied predicate, not a prepositional object: the bāʾ gives it genitive form while the clause denies the attribute of the divine speaker. Its indefiniteness under negation rejects any instance of oppressor-character, and the faʿʿāl pattern makes the denied predicate habitual or intensive rather than a single ordinary wrong. The {{ar:ظ ل م}} ({{tr:ẓ-l-m}}) root-image adds the idea of misplacing judgment, while local grammar keeps darkness and accusation branches as background pressure. In the recurring justice formula with {{ar:لِلْعَبِيدِ}} ({{tr:li-l-ʿabīd}}), the word denies systemic or misallocating injustice toward servants (3:182, 8:51, 22:10, 41:46), and its tanwīn releases directly into the lām phrase that names them.

topics.headline: indefinite predicate denies any oppressor-instance
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the clause excludes the oppressor-description itself from the divine speaker, not merely one unjust act.
topics.reason: The adjective is the predicate of the nominal negation, indefinite under negation, and governed in form by the reinforcing bāʾ.

topics.headline: faʿʿāl pattern makes the denied predicate intensive
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees that the negated term is the heavy habitual-oppressor form, so the denial reaches settled, repeated, or excessive wronging.
topics.reason: The local form is ADJ_INTENS on the faʿʿāl pattern, and occurrence evidence marks it as a specialized form inside a common root.

topics.headline: misplacement image sharpens justice without replacing the local sense
topics.reader_payoff: The reader understands injustice here as judgment put where it does not belong, while darkness and accusation derivatives remain supporting imagery rather than the selected local sense.
topics.reason: The root family supplies misplacement and darkness imagery, but the surface word is the intensive oppressor predicate in a negated justice formula.

topics.headline: fixed servant-justice formula anchors the predicate
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the word as part of a recurring divine-justice denial with the servant phrase, here placed after the immutable-decree clause (3:182, 8:51, 22:10, 41:46).
topics.reason: Occurrence and pair evidence show the intensive adjective repeatedly joined to the servant complement in divine justice contexts.

topics.headline: predicate seals shift from procedure to divine attribute
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices the ayah move from the status of a decree to an attribute-level justice declaration whose sound carries into the servant complement.
topics.reason: Boundary and convergence rows show the predicate as the turning point from immutable word to non-oppressive character.

words.gloss_range: relational or disadvantage lām specifying the affected party of the denied oppression, not ownership

supporting_anchors.gloss_range: fused lām phrase naming the affected class

words.prose: {{ar:لِ}} ({{tr:li}}) turns the denied adjective into a directed justice relation: the oppression being denied is wrong toward a party, not a free-floating quality. It governs {{ar:ٱلْعَبِيدِ}} ({{tr:al-ʿabīd}}) and fuses with the article in {{ar:لِلْعَبِيدِ}} ({{tr:li-l-ʿabīd}}), visibly and audibly binding the target relation to the servant class. Coming after the intensive predicate, the lām phrase completes the ayah's final justice frame.

topics.headline: lām marks the harmed-party relation
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that injustice is denied as wrong directed toward servants, not as an abstract quality with no affected party.
topics.reason: Attachment evidence makes the lām phrase the complement specifying the class toward whom the denied wrong would be directed.

topics.headline: proclitic fuses relation to servant noun
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees and hears the target relation attached to the servant noun, tightening the link between predicate and affected class.
topics.reason: The written proclitic and sound transition keep the relational complement bound to the final noun.

topics.headline: postposed lām phrase completes the predicate tail
topics.reader_payoff: The reader feels the clause first deny oppressor-character, then complete the denial by naming the affected domain.
topics.reason: The lām phrase follows the predicate and supplies its required complement.

words.gloss_range: the servants as a definite plural class governed by lām; locally the affected class toward whom oppression is denied
words.root_gloss_range: worship, service, servitude, dependency, and subjection field; local noun selects dependent servants as a class, with servitude-register pressure stronger than an honorific active-worshipper label

supporting_anchors.gloss_range: recurring denied-oppression formula with servant complement

words.prose: {{ar:ٱلْعَبِيدِ}} ({{tr:al-ʿabīd}}) supplies the endpoint of the justice relation: the clause is not only that the speaker is not an oppressor, but that He is not an oppressor toward the servant class. The definite plural makes the class generic and inclusive, while the chosen plural register foregrounds dependency and power-asymmetry rather than an honorific active-worshipper label. It completes the recurring {{ar:بِظَلَّٰمٍ لِلْعَبِيدِ}} ({{tr:bi-ẓallāmin li-l-ʿabīd}}) justice formula (3:182, 8:51, 22:10, 41:46), returns Surah Qaf's servant vocabulary from signs and provision into judgment (50:8, 50:11), and gives the protected class the ayah's final word with the long ending as its acoustic landing.

topics.headline: servant noun completes the affected complement
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the final noun is grammatically tied to the denied predicate as the affected class, not an independent subject or possession phrase.
topics.reason: The noun is genitive under lām and supplies the complement specifying toward whom oppression is denied.

topics.headline: definite plural universalizes the protected class
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the denial extend to servants as a class, not merely to a named subset in the immediate scene.
topics.reason: The definite plural under lām is generic in force and functions as the patient side of the justice relation.

topics.headline: ʿabīd foregrounds dependency and asymmetry
topics.reader_payoff: The reader feels the force of naming dependents under authority, which makes the denial of oppression more pointed than a neutral worshipper label would.
topics.reason: The root family spans worship, service, and subjugation; locally the concrete plural names dependent servants, while derivative enslavement actions remain background pressure.

topics.headline: final noun completes formula and surah-local return
topics.reader_payoff: The reader sees the servant noun complete a recurring divine-justice formula (3:182, 8:51, 22:10, 41:46) and bring earlier Surah Qaf servant language into the judgment scene (50:8, 50:11).
topics.reason: Formula and same-surah recurrence rows support the inter-ayah payoff without changing the local complement grammar.

topics.headline: final position lands the guarantee on the servants
topics.reader_payoff: The reader notices that the ayah ends not on the divine I or the oppressor predicate, but on the class protected by the denial.
topics.reason: The final word position and cadence make the servant class the closing landing of the justice guarantee.

baseline_models.focus_anchor: The passive yubaddalu governs al-qawl, followed by the denial of zulm toward al-abid.
baseline_models.mechanism: The saying is protected against both replacement and alteration of form; justice names the refusal to withhold what belongs to subjects under an asymmetric authority.

activation_trace.role: Replacement by another supplies the primary kind of change denied of the saying.
Alteration of a thing's form broadens the denial beyond simple substitution.
Speech brought out in utterance supplies the stable object of the denied change.
Withholding or blocking a right makes the justice denial operational rather than merely emotive.
Owned servants supply the unequal power relation in which non-withholding matters.

changed_reading.before: A general assertion that God's word and justice are constant.
changed_reading.after: No substitute or restyled pronouncement displaces the operative saying, and its constancy does not dispossess those subject to it.

baseline_models.focus_anchor: Ladayya places the unchangeable qawl in a presence where claims and complaints can be heard.
baseline_models.mechanism: Qawl can be negotiation or falsely attributed speech, while zulm can generate a complaint seeking redress; the line can therefore bar a party from swapping, renegotiating, or fabricating the speech before the authority.

activation_trace.role: Negotiation over an affair turns qawl into a possible pleading before an authority.
Attributing unsaid words supplies the risk of a fabricated or reassigned claim.
One thing taking another's place supplies the prohibited swap of pleadings.
A grievance and demand for equity gives the presence the shape of a redress forum.

changed_reading.before: The verse only declares an immutable divine decree.
changed_reading.after: The verse also sounds like a forum rule: speech cannot be exchanged, renegotiated, or put into another's mouth in the judging presence.

baseline_models.focus_anchor: The form-change branch of yubaddalu meets qawl as a thing's indication and zulm as misplacement.
baseline_models.mechanism: The denial may exclude changing a saying's outward presentation while claiming its underlying import is untouched, because a changed indication can move an application out of its proper place.

activation_trace.role: Changing form while a substance remains supplies semantic restyling rather than replacement.
A thing's saying as its indication lets altered presentation affect how the sign is read.
Putting something outside its proper place or time supplies the harm caused by distorted application.

changed_reading.before: No entirely different saying replaces the first.
changed_reading.after: Nor can the same saying be cosmetically recast so that its indication is applied elsewhere while its essence is claimed unchanged.

context_deltas.mechanism: Earlier speech exits the mouth, is guarded, and is presented ready; the sequence then stages competing companion speech and stops the dispute. The focus denial now protects docketed speech from post hoc editing.

activation_trace.role: Words physically brought out by the tongue establish an emitted evidentiary event.
The uttered qawl identifies the same speech category later protected from change.
Guarding and preservation give the emitted saying evidentiary custody.
Something present and prepared turns custody into ready presentation.
Contention between adversaries supplies the immediate litigation in which alteration is barred.
Substitution anchors the prohibition against replacing the preserved speech.
Negotiated speech anchors the baseline forum model now revised by the record sequence.

structural_cues: The locative chain 50:18 لديه, 50:23 لدي, 50:28 لدي, and 50:29 لدي contracts custody, presentation, dispute, and the no-change rule into one scene.
context_deltas.reader_inference: The packet supplies emitted speech, guarding, ready presentation, and a halted dispute; I infer that their sequence makes the focus qawl an integrity-protected record. A live alternative is that qawl remains only the prior divine warning, not creaturely evidence.

changed_reading.before: No plea can renegotiate a fixed pronouncement.
changed_reading.after: Once speech has been emitted, guarded, and presented in the final dispute, no party can swap or rewrite the record before the judge.

context_deltas.mechanism: The warning first becomes due and is then said to have been advanced beforehand. The unchanged saying is therefore a preannounced standard carried into judgment, not an improvised penalty.

activation_trace.role: A fixed obligation or due consequence supplies the warning's settled force.
Threat of harm identifies the negative commitment that becomes due.
Advancing something beforehand supplies notice prior to adjudication.
The repeated threat connects prior notice directly to the stopped dispute.
Denied substitution means the preannounced standard is not replaced at judgment.

structural_cues: The sequence moves from 50:14 فحق وعيد to 50:20 يوم الوعيد and 50:28 قدمت إليكم بالوعيد before the focus denial.
context_deltas.reader_inference: The packet supplies a warning that became due and was advanced earlier; I infer a non-retroactive judgment rule. The narrower alternative is one unalterable decree concerning Hell rather than a general procedural principle.

changed_reading.before: The saying is immutable simply because its speaker has absolute power.
changed_reading.after: The saying remains unchanged because judgment executes a consequence announced before the dispute, rather than inventing one after it.

context_deltas.mechanism: Servants receive allotted provision, the guilty party is marked as a withholder of good, and after the focus both a positive promise and an increase appear. Non-zulm thus protects promised benefit as well as constraining punishment; fixed commitment coexists with generosity beyond it.

activation_trace.role: An allotted gift establishes positive distribution to the servants.
The same servant relation as the focus receives provision before becoming the object of non-injustice.
Holding back the hand from giving marks the condemned human mechanism that divine non-zulm reverses.
A promise opening hope supplies the positive side of fulfilled speech.
Increase and growth show that invariant commitment need not cap additional generosity.
Withholding a right anchors non-injustice as protection against denied benefit.

structural_cues: Provision for servants precedes the condemned preventer of good; promised Garden and لدينا مزيد follow the fixed-word denial.
context_deltas.reader_inference: The packet supplies provision, condemned withholding, positive promise, and increase; I infer that the justice clause guarantees benefit as well as measured liability. The live alternative restricts al-qawl to the preceding threat and treats the reward sequence as separate.

changed_reading.before: Not being unjust means only that punishment is not excessive.
changed_reading.after: The same invariance also prevents promised good from being withheld from servants, while allowing an increase beyond what was promised.

context_deltas.mechanism: The accused is described through boundary-crossing and far error, while the closing instruction denies coercive compulsion and addresses one responsive to warning. The justice denial can therefore reject manufactured guilt: authority does not force a servant across the line and then punish the forced crossing.

activation_trace.role: Crossing a boundary and acting unjustly locates transgression in the accused conduct.
Departure from guidance supplies the condition attributed to the judged person amid the causation dispute.
Overpowering compulsion is explicitly denied as the messenger's mode.
Anticipatory fear marks a hearer capable of responding to warning rather than a coerced object.
Putting a thing in the wrong place anchors misassigned liability as injustice.
Making someone slave-like by subjection supplies the coercive relation the model tests against non-zulm.

structural_cues: In 50:27 the companion denies causing the person's transgression, and 50:45 opposes reminder to compulsion.
context_deltas.reader_inference: The packet supplies a disputed causal denial, boundary-crossing, error, and non-compulsive warning; I infer accountable response rather than manufactured guilt. 1. **The authoritative statement is neither substituted nor transformed.** `ب د ل:B001` supplies replacement and `ب د ل:B002` alteration; `ق و ل:B001` supplies uttered speech. The packet supplies contrasting distributions; I infer that “not unjust to the servants” denies arbitrary blockage of either claim or gift. The clause limits how authority is exercised: owned status does not license deprivation of what has become due.

facets.statement: Bir varlığın sayı, miktar veya ölçü bakımından çok olmayışıdır.
Azlık, kişinin yoksullaşması veya toplum içinde düşük ve değersiz görülmesi sonucuna uzanabilir.

Belirli olumsuzluk ve sıklık yapılarında hiç yokluğu veya bir eylemin pek seyrek gerçekleşmesini anlatır.
